ipo-calendar.interpretation: Deal size against the range is the read on demand: an upsized deal priced above the range is a different signal from one cut and priced below.
ipo-calendar.limits: Finnhub free coverage is inconsistent for smaller listings, withdrawn deals linger, and there is no post-listing performance tracking.
ipo-calendar.name: Price range, shares and expected proceeds

ipo-calendar.interpretation: A watchlist of supply coming to market. No enrichment, so it is a schedule rather than an analysis.
ipo-calendar.limits: Finnhub free coverage is inconsistent for smaller listings and withdrawn deals linger. No post-listing performance tracking.
ipo-calendar.name: Upcoming and recent IPOs

macro-cycle.interpretation: Plotted against the 2% target alongside core and PCE so the three can be read together rather than in isolation.
macro-cycle.limits: Headline includes food and energy and is therefore the noisiest of the three. The Fed does not target it.
macro-cycle.name: CPI year over year

macro-cycle.interpretation: The persistence read. Core moving while headline falls means the disinflation is energy, not demand.
macro-cycle.limits: Shelter is roughly a third of the basket and is measured with a long lag, so core turns later than the underlying reality.
macro-cycle.name: Core CPI year over year

macro-cycle.formula: current level minus prior month level, in thousands
macro-cycle.interpretation: Roughly 100k a month keeps pace with labour-force growth, which is the line the cycle panel scores against. The single most market-moving monthly release.
macro-cycle.limits: Revised twice and the revisions are frequently larger than the surprise that moved markets on the day. Establishment survey, so it counts jobs rather than people.
macro-cycle.name: Nonfarm payrolls

macro-cycle.formula: same, on the PCE price index
macro-cycle.interpretation: Structurally runs below CPI because of different weights and substitution assumptions. This is the series the 2% target actually refers to.
macro-cycle.limits: Released later than CPI and revised more. The core variant, not shown separately here, is the one the Fed cites.
macro-cycle.name: PCE year over year

macro-cycle.interpretation: The Fed half-mandate in one number, and the input to the Sahm gap in the cycle panel. The level matters less than the direction: unemployment rises non-linearly once it turns.
macro-cycle.limits: U-3 excludes discouraged workers and the underemployed. Household-survey based, so it is noisier month to month than payrolls.
macro-cycle.name: Unemployment rate

macro-cycle.formula: each component scored -1 to +1 by linear interpolation between a "good" and "bad" level; composite is the mean of whichever components resolved. Components: 10y-2y spread, initial claims vs their 12-month low, the Sahm gap (3-month unemployment average minus its prior 12-month minimum), 3-month average payroll growth, and the HY spread
macro-cycle.interpretation: Deliberately NOT a recession probability. Every component prints its level, its reading and the threshold it is judged against, so a reader who disagrees with one can see exactly which to discount. Currently Expansion at +0.46 with payrolls the single weak leg.
macro-cycle.limits: A hand-set scoring rule, not a fitted model, and no probability is claimed from it. Thresholds (Sahm 0.50pp, claims 15% above trough, HY 6 points) are documented rules of thumb, not estimated parameters. A dead feed narrows the base rather than scoring neutral, which would make the panel less decisive the more broken it got.
macro-cycle.name: Cycle position

macro-events.interpretation: The forward diary. Drives the macro_event_within_days alert, which can watch marquee movers, Fed/Treasury only, or everything high-importance.
macro-events.limits: Consensus is NOT in FRED. Expected figures come from an Investing.com scrape covering a subset of releases only, which is why an economic surprise index over the full calendar is not a free synthesis of data already held.
macro-events.name: Release schedule

macro-events.formula: same-day return of ^GSPC, DX-Y.NYB and ^TNX on the release date, from the shared price cache
macro-events.interpretation: Attaches a market consequence to a print, which is more useful than the print alone. Repeated large reactions mark which releases actually matter this cycle.
macro-events.limits: Whole-day returns, so it attributes everything that happened that day to the release. A release at 08:30 shares its day with the rest of the session.
macro-events.name: Release-day cross-asset reaction

market-compare.formula: indexed: price / price_at_window_start * 100; pct: price / base - 1
market-compare.interpretation: Indexing to 100 is the honest way to compare instruments of different price. Multiples and ratios plot on a separate right axis at their real level, because normalising a P/E destroys the thing you wanted to see.
market-compare.limits: Indexing is sensitive to the start date: shifting the window start changes every line. Price return only, so a high-yield asset is understated against a low-yield one over long windows.
market-compare.name: Normalised multi-asset comparison

master-valuation.formula: recompute the blend across a 2-D grid (discount rate, CAGR and margin, growth and risk, or margin and EV/EBITDA); outline the current model cell
master-valuation.interpretation: The most honest output in the valuation hub: it shows the range the model supports rather than a single number. If the grid spans 2x, the point estimate is not a price target.
master-valuation.limits: Two dimensions at a time, so interactions with a third assumption are invisible. The grid bounds are chosen, not derived, so the visible range is itself an assumption.
master-valuation.name: Sensitivity grid

master-valuation.formula: weighted mean of the enabled methods; weights renormalise over methods that produced a value (active_weights)
master-valuation.interpretation: The blend forces the disagreement between methods into the open. Effective weights are shown separately from requested weights, so a method that failed to produce a value does not silently drag the blend.
master-valuation.limits: Averaging four models does not reduce the error if they share an input, and they do: three of the four use the same share count and net debt. A confident-looking blend can rest on one bad balance sheet.
master-valuation.name: Blended fair value

master-valuation.formula: weighted mean over methods that produced a value, using renormalised active weights
master-valuation.interpretation: Effective weights are displayed separately from requested weights, so a method that failed to produce a value visibly drops out instead of silently dragging the blend toward zero.
master-valuation.limits: Averaging four models does not reduce error when they share inputs, and three of the four use the same share count and net debt. A confident blend can rest on one bad balance sheet.
master-valuation.name: Blended value

master-valuation.formula: Gordon growth or multi-stage: PV = sum(D_t/(1+r)^t) + terminal D(1+g)/(r-g)
master-valuation.interpretation: Only meaningful for a mature payer with a stable policy. For those it is the most direct valuation available because the cash flow to the shareholder is observed rather than modelled.
master-valuation.limits: Useless for non-payers and misleading for irregular payers. Requires r > g. Buybacks, which are the dominant return-of-capital route for US large caps, are invisible to it.
master-valuation.name: Dividend discount value

master-valuation.formula: retrieval over filing text, summarised by the LLM stack
master-valuation.interpretation: Grounds the assumptions in the actual filing rather than in the modeller priors. Dismissible, and never writes an assumption on its own.
master-valuation.limits: Generated text over retrieved passages: it can miss context and can restate a risk factor boilerplate as a finding. Nothing here changes a number unless a human accepts it.
master-valuation.name: Filing evidence, risks and watch items

master-valuation.formula: solve for the revenue growth that makes the DCF output equal the market price, holding other assumptions fixed
master-valuation.interpretation: Reframes the question from "what is it worth" to "what does the market already believe", which is a far more answerable question. Compare the implied rate against the company own history and the industry.
master-valuation.limits: Inherits every DCF assumption. Solving for one variable while holding the rest fixed attributes all disagreement to growth, when it may live in the margin or the discount rate.
master-valuation.name: Implied expectations

master-valuation.formula: sum of discounted FCFF plus discounted terminal value, less net debt, per diluted share
master-valuation.interpretation: The only leg that does not depend on other companies being priced correctly, which is its whole argument.
master-valuation.limits: Also the leg with the most assumptions, and terminal value dominates it. Independence from the market is bought with dependence on the modeller.
master-valuation.name: Intrinsic DCF value

master-valuation.formula: each selected target multiple applied to the matching company metric, blended by the target weights
master-valuation.interpretation: Market-anchored and fast. The spread across targets tells you whether the peer set actually agrees.
master-valuation.limits: Assumes the peer group is fairly valued, which is precisely what is in question during a bubble or a washout.
master-valuation.name: Market multiples value

master-valuation.interpretation: The output the whole tool exists to produce. Read it against the sensitivity grid: if the grid spans 2x, a 20% gap is inside the noise of the model.
master-valuation.limits: A gap is a statement about the assumptions, not about the market. The Reverse DCF tool inverts the question and is usually the more disciplined way to ask it.
master-valuation.name: Market price vs blended value

master-valuation.formula: peer median multiple x company metric (earnings, EBITDA, sales, book), converted to per-share equity value
master-valuation.interpretation: Fast and market-anchored. The spread between methods (P/E vs EV/EBITDA vs P/S) is informative: a wide spread means the capital structure or the margin profile differs from the peers.
master-valuation.limits: Assumes the peer group is fairly valued, which is exactly what is in question in a bubble or a washout. Meaningless on negative earnings, and the tool suppresses rather than prints those.
master-valuation.name: Peer-multiple implied value

master-valuation.formula: per-segment revenue share x segment multiple, summed, less net debt, per share
master-valuation.interpretation: The right frame for a conglomerate, where a blended multiple is meaningless. Reported segments load automatically so the starting point is the company own disclosure rather than a guess.
master-valuation.limits: Segment disclosure is coarse and inconsistent between companies. Revenue shares normalise to 100%, so an omitted segment silently inflates the rest. No conglomerate discount is applied.
master-valuation.name: Segment-based value

master-valuation.formula: seeded from the latest reported TTM revenue
master-valuation.interpretation: Everything downstream scales off this one number, so a wrong base is the most expensive input error available.
master-valuation.limits: Seeded from TTM, which lags a turn. For a company mid-acquisition the base is pre-deal unless overridden.
master-valuation.name: Base revenue

master-valuation.formula: EBIT x (1 - tax) + D&A - capex - change in working capital
master-valuation.interpretation: The actual thing being discounted. The reconciliation from margin to cash is where capital intensity shows up, and it is the step most skipped.
master-valuation.limits: Working capital is modelled as a share of revenue rather than from the individual line items, so a business with unusual payables dynamics is mis-modelled.
master-valuation.name: Cash from profit (FCFF)

master-valuation.formula: equity value = enterprise value - net debt; per share = equity value / diluted shares
master-valuation.interpretation: The unglamorous step where a good enterprise valuation becomes a wrong per-share number. Dilution from options and converts is frequently understated.
master-valuation.limits: Diluted share count is as reported and excludes announced but unissued dilution. Net debt uses period-end cash, which is seasonal for many businesses.
master-valuation.name: Net debt and diluted shares

master-valuation.formula: user rate, faded toward terminal growth over the horizon
master-valuation.interpretation: The single assumption the output is most sensitive to after WACC. Sanity-check it against the company own history and the industry, both of which are on the page.
master-valuation.limits: A constant CAGR is a fiction for any real business. The fade toward terminal growth softens it but the shape is still imposed rather than modelled.
master-valuation.name: Revenue CAGR

master-valuation.formula: g in TV = FCFF_final x (1+g) / (WACC - g)
master-valuation.interpretation: Terminal value is typically 60-80% of total DCF value, so this single number dominates the answer. Anything above long-run nominal GDP is a claim the company grows forever faster than the economy.
master-valuation.limits: The model is hypersensitive here: the gap (WACC - g) sits in a denominator, so small changes produce large swings as the two converge.
master-valuation.name: Terminal growth

master-valuation.formula: linear glide from the current margin to the terminal target across the horizon
master-valuation.interpretation: Where most optimism hides. A terminal margin above the best year the company or its industry has ever posted is the most common way a DCF is talked into a target price.
master-valuation.limits: Damodaran industry data is available as a reality check but is not enforced. Nothing prevents an unattainable value.
master-valuation.name: Terminal margin

master-valuation.formula: cost of equity from CAPM (risk free + beta x ERP) blended with after-tax cost of debt at target weights
master-valuation.interpretation: Together with terminal growth it usually moves fair value more than any operating assumption, which is why the sensitivity grid defaults to this axis.
master-valuation.limits: Must exceed terminal growth or the perpetuity formula diverges and the model is nonsense. Beta silently backstops from the bundled Damodaran snapshot when the vendor has none.
master-valuation.name: WACC

monte-carlo.formula: roots of the expiry payoff function across the price grid
monte-carlo.interpretation: The deterministic frame around the probabilistic result. Distance from spot to the nearest break-even is the honest read on how much has to go right.
monte-carlo.limits: Expiry-only: ignores the path, early assignment and financing. A structure can be profitable at expiry and still be closed at a loss on a margin call.
monte-carlo.name: Break-even prices

monte-carlo.formula: the strategy evaluated on the realised price series rather than on simulated ones
monte-carlo.interpretation: The control for the simulation. A large gap between replay and median simulated return means the model assumptions, not the strategy, are producing the result.
monte-carlo.limits: A single path, so it is an anecdote by construction. Included as a sanity check, not as evidence.
monte-carlo.name: Exact replay return

monte-carlo.formula: minimum and maximum of the expiry payoff across the evaluated price grid
monte-carlo.interpretation: Max loss is the number that should size the position, not probability of profit. A 70% win rate with a 5:1 loss ratio is a losing structure.
monte-carlo.limits: Bounded by the evaluated grid, so an unbounded short leg shows a finite max loss that is an artefact of the grid width rather than a real limit.
monte-carlo.name: Max loss and max profit

monte-carlo.interpretation: The central case. Reported as a median rather than a mean because terminal wealth of a compounding series is right-skewed and the mean sits above almost every path.
monte-carlo.limits: Inherits the drift assumption directly. If drift is estimated from the same history being simulated, this is close to circular.
monte-carlo.name: Median final value

monte-carlo.formula: median of the per-path maximum drawdown
monte-carlo.interpretation: More useful than a single historical drawdown because it is a distribution: it answers "what drawdown should I expect", not "what happened once".
monte-carlo.limits: Only as good as the path generator. GBM cannot produce clustered volatility, so its drawdowns are systematically too shallow.
monte-carlo.name: Median max drawdown

monte-carlo.formula: median across paths of the maximum margin requirement as a share of equity
monte-carlo.interpretation: The early-warning number for a levered structure: a book that peaks at 90% utilisation on the median path will breach on plenty of others.
monte-carlo.limits: Peak is per-path, so the median peak is not the peak of the median path and cannot be read off the equity fan.
monte-carlo.name: Median peak margin

monte-carlo.interpretation: The width between them is the real output. A band spanning 5x means the horizon is too long or the volatility too high for any point estimate to be meaningful.
monte-carlo.limits: Tail quantiles need far more paths to stabilise than the median. A run with few paths shows a steady median and a jittery band.
monte-carlo.name: P5 and P95 outcomes

monte-carlo.interpretation: The most intuitive output and the easiest to over-read. For an options structure it is the headline, but a 70% win probability with a 5:1 loss ratio is a losing trade.
monte-carlo.limits: Says nothing about magnitude. Always read beside max loss and CVaR, which is why they are on the same strip.
monte-carlo.name: Probability of profit

monte-carlo.formula: count(paths breaching ruin or the maintenance requirement) / paths * 100
monte-carlo.interpretation: The constraint that makes median outcomes irrelevant: a path that liquidates cannot recover, so leverage turns a good median into a bad expectation.
monte-carlo.limits: Depends on user-entered maintenance percentages. Assumes no top-up and no discretionary deleveraging, which is conservative but not always realistic.
monte-carlo.name: Probability of ruin and forced liquidation

monte-carlo.formula: arithmetic mean return - geometric mean return, approximately variance / 2
monte-carlo.interpretation: Explains why a strategy with a positive average return can still lose money. The drag grows with the square of volatility, which is the mathematical case against leverage.
monte-carlo.limits: The variance/2 approximation breaks down at high volatility, where the true drag is larger than the formula suggests.
monte-carlo.name: Volatility drag

monte-carlo.formula: physical GBM uses estimated drift; risk-neutral sets drift to the risk-free rate; Student-t adds a tail degrees-of-freedom parameter; block bootstrap resamples real returns in 10-day blocks
monte-carlo.interpretation: Risk-neutral is the correct choice for pricing an option structure; physical is the correct choice for forecasting a portfolio. Using the wrong one is the most common error this selector prevents.
monte-carlo.limits: The same structure produces materially different probability-of-profit under each. The choice is exposed rather than hidden precisely because it is not neutral.
monte-carlo.name: Simulation model

monte-carlo.formula: count of paths hitting the stop, the target, or running to the horizon
monte-carlo.interpretation: The distribution of exit reasons is the clearest picture of whether the exit rules are doing anything. If 95% of paths hold to cap, the stop is decorative.
monte-carlo.limits: Stops are evaluated at bar close, so a path that would have gapped through a stop is filled at the stop level rather than at the gap.
monte-carlo.name: Stop-loss, take-profit and hold-to-cap outcomes

mover.formula: stock return minus benchmark return over the same session
mover.interpretation: Strips out the day beta. A 4% move on a 3% market day is a much smaller story than the headline number suggests.
mover.limits: Simple difference rather than a beta-adjusted residual, so a high-beta name shows spurious excess return on a large market day.
mover.name: Excess return vs the market

mover.formula: z = (today return - mean) / stdev over the trailing window; relative volume = today volume / 20-day average
mover.interpretation: A z-score above 2 with no evidence found is itself the finding: the move is not explained by anything public. Relative volume separates a real move from a thin-tape drift.
mover.limits: The trailing distribution includes the current regime, so during a volatile period everything looks normal. Relative volume is distorted by index rebalance days.
mover.name: Move z-score and relative volume

mover.formula: z_score of the day return against a trailing distribution; relative_volume against a 20-day average; excess return vs the market
mover.interpretation: Separates a real catalyst from noise. A z-score above 2 with no evidence found is itself informative: it says the move is not explained by anything public.
mover.limits: The LLM synthesis is a summary of the evidence listed below it, and when the summarizer is unavailable the page shows the raw evidence rather than nothing. Social coverage is limited by the same dead Reddit path as the sentiment tool.
mover.name: Why a name is moving

news.formula: stock return minus benchmark return over the same session
news.interpretation: Strips out the day beta. A 4% move on a 3% market day is a much smaller story than the headline number suggests.
news.limits: Simple difference rather than a beta-adjusted residual, so a high-beta name shows spurious excess return on a large market day.
news.name: Excess return vs the market

news.formula: z = (today return - mean) / stdev over the trailing window; relative volume = today volume / 20-day average
news.interpretation: A z-score above 2 with no evidence found is itself the finding: the move is not explained by anything public. Relative volume separates a real move from a thin-tape drift.
news.limits: The trailing distribution includes the current regime, so during a volatile period everything looks normal. Relative volume is distorted by index rebalance days.
news.name: Move z-score and relative volume

news.formula: z_score of the day return against a trailing distribution; relative_volume against a 20-day average; excess return vs the market
news.interpretation: Separates a real catalyst from noise. A z-score above 2 with no evidence found is itself informative: it says the move is not explained by anything public.
news.limits: The LLM synthesis is a summary of the evidence listed below it, and when the summarizer is unavailable the page shows the raw evidence rather than nothing. Social coverage is limited by the same dead Reddit path as the sentiment tool.
news.name: Why a name is moving

options.formula: ATM IV minus annualised 30-day realised volatility (the IV premium)
options.interpretation: The variance risk premium in one number. Persistently positive is the structural norm; a negative reading means options are cheap relative to how the stock is actually moving.
options.limits: Compares a forward-looking implied number against a backward-looking realised one over different windows, which is standard practice but not an apples-to-apples comparison.
options.name: IV against realised volatility

options.formula: iv_rank = (current - min) / (max - min) * 100; iv_percentile = share of days below current * 100
options.interpretation: Rank answers "how expensive is vol against its own year" and is the standard trigger for premium selling above ~50 and buying below ~20. Percentile is the more robust of the two because a single spike sets the range that rank divides by. Also available as an alert condition.
options.limits: Both need a year of accrued snapshots; a ticker only recently tracked has a short and therefore flattering range. There is no historical IV surface from any current vendor, so the series starts when this app started recording it, not when the option started trading.
options.name: IV rank and IV percentile

options.formula: ATM IV per expiry across up to 16 expiries, with the front-to-back slope
options.interpretation: Backwardation, where the front is above the back, marks an event or a stress. Contango is the resting state. The slope figure is what the scanner sorts on.
options.limits: Chain-derived and point-in-time. Expiries are unevenly spaced, so the slope between adjacent expiries is not a constant-maturity measure.
options.name: Term structure

options.formula: per-strike IV from the chain, normalised through one shared _normalize_iv rule; 25-delta risk reversal and butterfly reported alongside
options.interpretation: A steep put skew means downside protection is bid, which is normal for an index and a signal in a single name. The 25-delta risk reversal is the compact numeric version of the same read.
options.limits: IV is normalised by one shared rule because the two sources quote it differently; before that fix the same contract could read 25% in one pane and 0% in another. No historical surface, so today skew cannot be compared with its own history.
options.name: Volatility skew

options.formula: first derivative of BS price with respect to spot
options.interpretation: The hedge ratio, and loosely the risk-neutral probability of finishing in the money. Aggregating it across legs gives the structure directional exposure.
options.limits: Loses meaning as a probability under a skewed surface, which is exactly when people reach for it.
options.name: Delta

options.formula: second derivative of BS price with respect to spot
options.interpretation: How fast the hedge goes wrong. Largest at the money and near expiry, which is why short-dated ATM positions are the dangerous ones.
options.limits: Assumes constant volatility, so it understates the true convexity when vol moves with spot.
options.name: Gamma

options.formula: derivative of BS price with respect to the risk-free rate
options.interpretation: Negligible for short-dated equity options and material for LEAPS, which is the only time it is worth reading.
options.limits: Uses a single flat rate rather than a term structure.
options.name: Rho

options.formula: closed-form BS on spot, strike, time to expiry, rate, volatility and type
options.interpretation: The reference against the market mid. A persistent gap is usually the IV input, not a mispricing.
options.limits: European exercise with no dividends. US single-name equity options are American, so the model is wrong for deep in-the-money puts and around ex-dividend dates.
options.name: Theoretical price

options.formula: derivative of BS price with respect to time, per calendar day
options.interpretation: The carry cost of being long options and the income of being short. Accelerates into expiry rather than running linearly.
options.limits: Quoted per calendar day while decay actually concentrates around trading sessions, so a weekend overstates the daily figure.
options.name: Theta

options.formula: derivative of BS price with respect to volatility
options.interpretation: The volatility exposure. Two structures with identical delta can have opposite vega, which decides how they behave through an event.
options.limits: Assumes a parallel shift in the surface. Real vol moves are not parallel, so a vega number across expiries overstates hedge accuracy.
options.name: Vega

options-unusual.formula: volume / open_interest per contract, filtered by min_volume and min_vol_oi thresholds
options-unusual.interpretation: A ratio above 1 means more contracts traded today than were outstanding, which is the standard screen for new positioning rather than closing trades. Grouped by underlying so a name appearing on several strikes is visible as one story.
options-unusual.limits: This is the whole of what the tool calls "flow". Sweep, block and premium tagging are NOT derivable: Tradier returns 11 fields and volume is a daily aggregate with no trade-level prints, so the tagging column was removed rather than fabricated. Real flow tagging needs an OPRA-derived vendor. Tradier failures fall back to the chain and are reported per symbol in a `failed` map.
options-unusual.name: Volume / open interest ratio

pairs.formula: statistical test for a stationary linear combination of the two price series
pairs.interpretation: The gate that decides whether mean reversion is a reasonable expectation at all, rather than a curve fit. Without it a pairs trade is two correlated bets.
pairs.limits: Cointegration over a chosen window frequently fails out of sample. A pair can test cointegrated historically and be structurally broken today, and no test distinguishes those.
pairs.name: Cointegration test

pairs.formula: OLS of A on B gives beta; spread = A - beta x B
pairs.interpretation: The spread is the tradable series, not either leg. A hedge ratio far from 1 means the position is materially unbalanced in dollar terms.
pairs.limits: An OLS hedge ratio is unstable and drifts; it is estimated over the whole window rather than rolling, so a structural break is averaged away.
pairs.name: Hedge ratio and spread

pairs.interpretation: The entry and exit trigger. Conventional thresholds are 2 to enter and 0 to exit, both visible on the chart.
pairs.limits: Assumes the spread is stationary. If the pair has genuinely decoupled, the z-score keeps signalling entry all the way down.
pairs.name: Spread z-score

peer-valuation.formula: per-peer multiples from financials; peer set from sector/industry match
peer-valuation.interpretation: The relative-value read: where a name sits against its own peer group rather than against its own history. Read the median, not the mean, since one loss-making peer distorts a P/E average.
peer-valuation.limits: Peer selection is by classification, not by business model, so a diversified company gets an incoherent set. Multiples on negative earnings are suppressed rather than shown as negative. Free-tier FMP caps enrichment, so some peers fall back to the bundled seed.
peer-valuation.name: Trading comps

peer-valuation.formula: peer median multiple x company metric (earnings, EBITDA, sales, book), converted to per-share equity value
peer-valuation.interpretation: Fast and market-anchored. The spread between methods (P/E vs EV/EBITDA vs P/S) is informative: a wide spread means the capital structure or the margin profile differs from the peers.
peer-valuation.limits: Assumes the peer group is fairly valued, which is exactly what is in question in a bubble or a washout. Meaningless on negative earnings, and the tool suppresses rather than prints those.
peer-valuation.name: Peer-multiple implied value

portfolio.interpretation: Turns a price-return book into something closer to total return. Ex-dates matter for anyone hedging around them.
portfolio.limits: Historical dividends only; a forward estimate is an extrapolation of the last declared rate. Special dividends distort a trailing yield badly.
portfolio.name: Dividends

portfolio.formula: sum(shares * price) recomputed on each poll and appended to an in-session series
portfolio.interpretation: Shows the day path rather than just the endpoint. The axis is deliberately a fixed numeric time axis with a stable value domain, because auto-scaling on a polling chart makes the line appear to jump on every tick.
portfolio.limits: In-session only and not persisted, so a refresh restarts the curve. Built from polled marks, so a gap in polling appears as a straight line rather than as missing data.
portfolio.name: Intraday book-value curve

portfolio.formula: shares * live price; weight = position value / book value
portfolio.interpretation: The live cockpit. Weight here is the input the Allocator rebalance reads as the current state.
portfolio.limits: Options and futures are marked on a separate path and are excluded from the weighted equity legs handed to other tools, surfaced as a note rather than dropped silently.
portfolio.name: Market value and weight per position

portfolio.formula: shares * (price - avg cost); return = price / avg cost - 1
portfolio.interpretation: Cost basis is user-entered, so this is only as accurate as what was typed. Imported books carry the basis from the import where the source had one.
portfolio.limits: No lot-level tracking, so a position built in several tranches shows one blended basis and cannot produce tax-lot reporting.
portfolio.name: Unrealized P&L and return

portfolio.interpretation: The input every portfolio tool keys off. Books are importable into Allocator, Analysis, Compare, Backtester, Factor Decomposition and the drawdown alert through PMImportPicker.
portfolio.limits: localStorage only, so it is per browser and never synced server-side. A drawdown alert therefore has to carry its holdings in the alert payload, the same way a strategy alert carries its rules. Clearing site data deletes the book.
portfolio.name: Holdings, options, futures and cash

portfolio-backtest.interpretation: A strategy in cash most of the time posts low volatility for a reason that has nothing to do with skill. Read alongside time-in-market.
portfolio-backtest.limits: Computed over all bars including flat ones, so a rarely-traded strategy looks far calmer than it is when actually positioned.
portfolio-backtest.name: Annualized volatility

portfolio-backtest.interpretation: The ratio most aligned with whether a strategy is actually holdable through its bad period.
portfolio-backtest.limits: One historical drawdown sets the denominator, so the figure changes discontinuously when the window crosses a crash.
portfolio-backtest.name: Calmar

portfolio-backtest.formula: intercept of the OLS of strategy daily returns on benchmark daily returns
portfolio-backtest.interpretation: The excess the strategy produced per day after accounting for its market exposure. Annualise it mentally by multiplying by roughly 252 to judge whether it is material.
portfolio-backtest.limits: No t-statistic or p-value is reported on this panel, so there is nothing here to distinguish alpha from luck. The Regression tools do report significance; this does not.
portfolio-backtest.name: Daily alpha

portfolio-backtest.formula: Pearson r between strategy and benchmark daily returns, and its square
portfolio-backtest.interpretation: A high R-squared means the strategy is a levered or delevered index position whatever its rules claim. Low correlation with positive alpha is the only combination worth paying for.
portfolio-backtest.limits: Measures linear co-movement only. A strategy that is flat most of the time and fully long occasionally can show low R-squared while carrying full market risk when it matters.
portfolio-backtest.name: Market correlation and R-squared

portfolio-backtest.interpretation: The number that decides whether a backtest is investable. A 25% CAGR with a 70% drawdown is a strategy nobody holds to the recovery.
portfolio-backtest.limits: Close-to-close on the bar interval, so intraday depth and any stop that would have triggered inside a bar are invisible.
portfolio-backtest.name: Max drawdown

portfolio-backtest.formula: size array clamped to [0,1], NaN to 0; position value = cash * allocation * size[i]
portfolio-backtest.interpretation: Turns a binary signal into a conviction-weighted one. All three P&L engines honour it.
portfolio-backtest.limits: A wrong-shaped size array raises 422 rather than being broadcast, deliberately: silently recycling a short array would misalign every subsequent bar.
portfolio-backtest.name: Per-bar position sizing

portfolio-backtest.formula: mean(strategy daily return) / stdev(strategy daily return) * sqrt(bars_per_year)
portfolio-backtest.interpretation: The standard comparator across strategies on the same instrument. Anything above 2 on a daily-bar backtest of a simple rule set should be assumed to be overfitting until proven otherwise.
portfolio-backtest.limits: No risk-free subtraction in this engine, so it is a raw information-ratio-style figure and reads high against a textbook Sharpe in a high-rate environment.
portfolio-backtest.name: Sharpe ratio

portfolio-backtest.interpretation: The right ratio for a trend strategy, whose whole design is to have lumpy upside and clipped downside.
portfolio-backtest.limits: Downside deviation on a sparse trade count is estimated from very few observations and is correspondingly unstable.
portfolio-backtest.name: Sortino

portfolio-backtest.interpretation: Makes windows of different length comparable. The paired Portfolio CAGR column is the same figure for the underlying held passively.
portfolio-backtest.limits: Annualising a short backtest is the most common way to make noise look like edge. Under about three years it says very little.
portfolio-backtest.name: Strategy CAGR

portfolio-backtest.interpretation: The raw result before any risk adjustment. Always read against the buy-and-hold line on the same chart: a strategy that underperforms holding is not a strategy.
portfolio-backtest.limits: No commission, slippage, spread or borrow. Fills are at the close of the signal bar, which is unachievable in practice and flatters any signal that keys off the close.
portfolio-backtest.name: Total return

portfolio-backtest.formula: count of entry-to-exit pairs; mean bars held, converted to days
portfolio-backtest.interpretation: The sample size behind every other statistic here. Fewer than about 30 trades means the Sharpe and win rate are anecdotes.
portfolio-backtest.limits: A high trade count on daily bars implies costs this engine does not model, so the more trades a strategy makes the more optimistic its result.
portfolio-backtest.name: Trades and average hold

portfolio-backtest.interpretation: Almost useless alone and routinely misread. A 35% win rate with 4:1 winners beats a 70% win rate with 1:3, which is why the P&L and average-hold columns sit next to it.
portfolio-backtest.limits: Sensitive to how a trade is defined: this engine closes a trade on the exit signal, so a strategy that scales out registers differently from one that exits at once.
portfolio-backtest.name: Win rate

portfolio-backtest.formula: rule blocks compile to Python through backend/algo_runtime/compiler.py; generated code runs in an AST-allowlist sandbox on a forkserver process with resource limits
portfolio-backtest.interpretation: Both paths produce the same (entries, exits, size) contract, so a strategy can move between the visual builder and code without changing the P&L engine. Saved strategies carry a PY badge showing which path is active.
portfolio-backtest.limits: Generated code is validated at seven levels including a causality check by future perturbation (rewriting data after bar k and confirming earlier output is byte-identical), which catches lookahead that prefix truncation misses. Validation rejects genuine lookahead but cannot prove a strategy is economically sound.
portfolio-backtest.name: Rule and Python strategy signals

portfolio-optimizer.formula: current shares = (baseline weight/100 x book value)/price; target the same at the slider weights; delta = target - current; trades filtered to |drift| >= 0.1pp
portfolio-optimizer.interpretation: Turns an optimiser output into something actionable. Turnover is shown alongside so the cost of the rebalance is visible before the trade list. A position exited to zero appears as a row rather than disappearing.
portfolio-optimizer.limits: No commission, spread, tax lot or wash-sale handling. Anything inside 0.1 percentage points is treated as noise and omitted. CSV export only: there is no hand-off to Paper Trading, because that bridge is options-only today.
portfolio-optimizer.name: Drift and rebalance trade list

portfolio-optimizer.formula: mean-variance optimisation across the ticker set under the chosen bounds
portfolio-optimizer.interpretation: The curve is the menu; a book plotted below it is giving up return for no reason. The shape matters more than any single point on it.
portfolio-optimizer.limits: Notoriously sensitive to the expected-return estimate. Small changes in the input move the whole curve, which is why the CAPM option exists as an alternative to raw historical means.
portfolio-optimizer.name: Efficient frontier

portfolio-optimizer.formula: the frontier point maximising (return - risk free) / volatility, with locked tickers held fixed and the remainder redistributed
portfolio-optimizer.interpretation: Locking positions and redistributing the rest is what makes this usable on a real book rather than a blank slate. The proposal feeds directly into the rebalance trade list.
portfolio-optimizer.limits: Concentrates aggressively into whichever asset had the best historical Sharpe, which is why bounds and locks exist. Unconstrained output is rarely investable.
portfolio-optimizer.name: Max-Sharpe portfolio and target weights

portfolio-risk.formula: stdev(daily returns) * sqrt(252) * 100
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The denominator of Sharpe and the plain measure of how bumpy the ride was. Above roughly 20% is equity-like; below 10% means significant bond or cash weight.
portfolio-risk.limits: Treats upside and downside deviation identically, which is why Sortino exists. Assumes returns are iid, so it understates risk for a trending or autocorrelated book.
portfolio-risk.name: Annualized volatility

portfolio-risk.formula: cov(book returns, benchmark returns) / var(benchmark returns)
portfolio-risk.interpretation: Above 1 means the book amplifies market moves. Read with the factor decomposition: a beta of 1 can hide offsetting sector and rate exposures.
portfolio-risk.limits: Contemporaneous OLS beta with no lead-lag correction, unlike the Global Markets asset panel. A book holding foreign equities will read low for the session-offset reason documented there.
portfolio-risk.name: Beta

portfolio-risk.formula: annualised return / |max drawdown|
portfolio-risk.interpretation: Answers "return per unit of the worst thing that actually happened", which is the number a drawdown-sensitive allocator cares about most.
portfolio-risk.limits: Driven entirely by a single historical event. A book that missed one crash by luck shows a flattering Calmar that says nothing about the next one.
portfolio-risk.name: Calmar

portfolio-risk.formula: marginal contribution to risk = weight * (covariance row . weights) / portfolio vol, normalised to 100%
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The gap between the two bars is the point. A 5% position supplying 20% of the risk is the position that will decide the outcome, regardless of what the weight says.
portfolio-risk.limits: Covariance is estimated over the chosen window and is unstable for short ones. Assumes a linear risk model, so it understates option and convexity exposure.
portfolio-risk.name: Capital weight vs risk contribution

portfolio-risk.formula: deterministic thresholds over concentration, covariance risk contribution, beta and historical return
portfolio-risk.interpretation: Deliberately deterministic so every flag can be traced to a rule. The page states plainly that these are review flags, not generated investment advice.
portfolio-risk.limits: Threshold-based, so it flags on level rather than on trajectory and will keep flagging a position that is already being fixed. No forward-looking input at all.
portfolio-risk.name: Downtrend watch and decision ledger

portfolio-risk.formula: HHI = sum(weight^2); effective holdings = 1 / HHI
portfolio-risk.interpretation: A 20-position book with an effective count of 4 is a 4-position book wearing a disguise. This is the fastest read on whether diversification is real.
portfolio-risk.limits: Counts positions, not risk: two names in the same sector count as two. The risk-contribution panel is the version that accounts for covariance.
portfolio-risk.name: HHI and effective holdings

portfolio-risk.formula: min(equity / cummax(equity) - 1) * 100
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The honest worst case an investor would have had to sit through. More predictive of whether someone actually holds a strategy than any return figure.
portfolio-risk.limits: Path-dependent and window-dependent: extending the window can only make it worse, never better. Uses closing values, so intraday depth is understated.
portfolio-risk.name: Max drawdown

portfolio-risk.formula: final value / initial value - 1
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The un-annualised number, which is the one that matches a brokerage statement over the same dates.
portfolio-risk.limits: Not comparable across windows of different length. Price return over the book; dividends are handled separately.
portfolio-risk.name: Period return

portfolio-risk.formula: (final/initial)^(252/observations) - 1
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The headline return, annualised so windows of different length compare. Read it beside Max drawdown: a 20% CAGR bought with a 60% drawdown is a different product from the same CAGR at 15%.
portfolio-risk.limits: Geometric, so it is dominated by the window endpoints. A window that starts at a crash low flatters it badly. Assumes the current weights were held throughout, with no rebalancing drag.
portfolio-risk.name: Portfolio CAGR

portfolio-risk.formula: sum of position weights grouped by sector
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The cross-check on a book that looks diversified by name count. Read it against the risk contribution panel rather than on its own.
portfolio-risk.limits: Sector tags come from yfinance own taxonomy, not GICS, and a conglomerate gets one tag. Cash, options and futures fall outside the sector split.
portfolio-risk.name: Sector allocation

portfolio-risk.formula: (annualised arithmetic return - risk free) / annualised vol
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The standard risk-adjusted comparator. Above 1 is good, above 2 is rare and usually means a short window or a hidden tail risk.
portfolio-risk.limits: Penalises upside volatility as heavily as downside. Highly unstable on under two years of data, and trivially gamed by a strategy that sells tails.
portfolio-risk.name: Sharpe

portfolio-risk.formula: each book valued as a weighted basket over history; the same metric set as Portfolio Analysis; liquidation flagged when levered equity goes to zero
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The A/B test for allocation decisions. Leverage and borrow rate are inputs, so the cost of a levered version is charged rather than assumed away, and a book that would have been liquidated is flagged rather than shown with a fictional recovery.
portfolio-risk.limits: Assumes fixed weights with no rebalancing drag or transaction cost. Borrow is a flat rate, not a term structure, so a long backtest under changing rates is optimistic or pessimistic depending on the period.
portfolio-risk.name: Side-by-side book comparison

portfolio-risk.formula: (annualised arithmetic return - risk free) / downside deviation
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The more honest ratio for an asymmetric book, because it stops punishing the volatility you want. A large Sortino/Sharpe gap means the book upside is lumpy, which is usually a feature.
portfolio-risk.limits: Downside deviation is estimated from fewer observations than total volatility, so it is noisier. Sensitive to the choice of minimum acceptable return, which is fixed at the risk-free rate here.
portfolio-risk.name: Sortino

portfolio-risk.formula: quantile(terminal returns, 0.05)
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The pessimistic planning case. Pair it with Liquidation odds: a bad percentile matters far more when leverage means the path cannot be held.
portfolio-risk.limits: Simulated, not historical. The tail is a model output, and the model assumptions are the input that moves it most.
portfolio-risk.name: 5th percentile outcome

portfolio-risk.formula: quantile(terminal returns, 0.95)
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The optimistic case, useful mainly as a width check: a very wide p5-to-p95 band means the horizon is too long or the vol too high for the median to mean much.
portfolio-risk.limits: Same model dependence as the downside. Right tail is less policy-relevant than the left but is quoted for symmetry.
portfolio-risk.name: 95th percentile outcome

portfolio-risk.formula: mean of the simulated terminal returns below the 5th percentile
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The number to actually read. Unlike VaR it is sensitive to the shape of the tail, so it distinguishes a book that loses 6% in a bad case from one that loses 40%.
portfolio-risk.limits: Entirely determined by the simulation model. A Gaussian engine cannot produce the fat tails that make real crashes, so CVaR from a GBM run is optimistic by construction.
portfolio-risk.name: CVaR 95

portfolio-risk.formula: intercept of the multivariate factor regression, annualised; rolling beta over an N-day window
portfolio-risk.interpretation: Alpha here means "unexplained by these five factors", not "skill". A rising rolling beta during a rally usually means the book is drifting more aggressive without anyone deciding to.
portfolio-risk.limits: Only five factors, with no size, value or momentum leg, so a style tilt reports as alpha. Alpha estimates need years of data to separate from noise and are rarely significant over a single year.
portfolio-risk.name: Factor alpha and rolling beta

portfolio-risk.formula: count(paths breaching the maintenance requirement) / total paths * 100
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The number that turns leverage from an abstraction into a probability. A book with an attractive median and 15% liquidation odds is not the same product as one at 0%.
portfolio-risk.limits: Depends on the long and short maintenance percentages entered, which are user inputs rather than broker-verified. Assumes no intra-path deleveraging or margin top-up.
portfolio-risk.name: Liquidation odds

portfolio-risk.formula: quantile(terminal returns, 0.50)
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The central expectation, and a better planning number than the mean because the terminal distribution of a compounding series is right-skewed.
portfolio-risk.limits: The median of a simulation is not a forecast. It inherits the drift assumption, which is usually estimated from the same history being simulated.
portfolio-risk.name: Median outcome

portfolio-risk.formula: percentile envelope of the simulated equity paths at each step
portfolio-risk.interpretation: Shows the cone widening with time, which is the single best visual argument that a long-horizon point forecast is meaningless.
portfolio-risk.limits: The cone is not a confidence interval on reality, only on the model. Correlations are held fixed across the horizon, which is exactly when they break.
portfolio-risk.name: Monte Carlo outcome fan

portfolio-risk.formula: 5th percentile of the simulated terminal return distribution
portfolio-risk.interpretation: Where the tail starts. Useful as a budget line, not as a worst case: by construction one path in twenty is worse than this, and VaR says nothing about how much worse.
portfolio-risk.limits: A quantile, so it is blind to everything beyond it. Two books with identical VaR can have wildly different disaster profiles, which is the whole reason CVaR sits next to it.
portfolio-risk.name: VaR 95

portfolio-risk.interpretation: Longer horizons widen the cone superlinearly. Path count affects only the smoothness of the percentile estimates, not their centre.
portfolio-risk.limits: Percentile estimates in the far tail need far more paths to stabilise than the median does, so a low path count makes CVaR noisy while the median looks fine.
portfolio-risk.name: Horizon and path count

portfolio-risk.formula: GBM draws iid lognormal; Student-t adds fat tails via a degrees-of-freedom parameter; block bootstrap resamples real historical returns in 10-day blocks
portfolio-risk.interpretation: The block bootstrap is the one to use for any drawdown question, because it preserves the serial correlation that produces real crashes. GBM structurally cannot generate them.
portfolio-risk.limits: Exposing the model is honest but shifts the burden: the same book can show very different CVaR under each. Bootstrap can only reproduce crashes already in the sample window.
portfolio-risk.name: Simulation model

price-history.interpretation: Turns an unexplained gap into a labelled one, which is the fastest way to rule a move in or out as a data artefact.
price-history.limits: Coverage depends on filing data and is sparse for non-US names. Split adjustment is applied to prices, so an unmarked historical split would show as a real move.
price-history.name: Corporate event markers

price-history.interpretation: The base layer. Alpaca supplies up to 119 days of 5-minute bars against yfinance 60-day cap, so intraday history is materially deeper when the key is set.
price-history.limits: Alpaca covers US equities and ETFs only; indices, futures, FX and crypto are screened out and served by yfinance or Binance. Feed is IEX, not full-market SIP, so volume is a fraction of consolidated tape.
price-history.name: OHLCV candles

price-history.formula: SMA(close, N) plus and minus k standard deviations of close over the same window
price-history.interpretation: Band width is a volatility read in itself: a squeeze usually precedes an expansion, regardless of direction.
price-history.limits: Assumes returns are normally distributed around the mean, which they are not, so touches of the band are more frequent than the nominal probability implies.
price-history.name: Bollinger bands

price-history.formula: net GEX and flip from the options exposure engine, resampled onto the chart timeline
price-history.interpretation: Putting the flip level on the same time axis as price is the point: it shows when price crossed into a negative-gamma regime rather than just that it is there now.
price-history.limits: Sparse relative to price, so the lane syncs one-way from the main chart and never back. A two-way sync would drag the price axis to the sparse series range.
price-history.name: Dealer GEX lane

price-history.formula: IV rank and percentile from the snapshot history, resampled onto the chart timeline
price-history.interpretation: Shows whether the current option pricing is unusual in the context of the plotted price move.
price-history.limits: Limited by the accrued snapshot history, which starts when this app began recording rather than when the option started trading.
price-history.name: IV rank and percentile lane

price-history.formula: indicators computed client-side in lib/indicators.ts over the fetched OHLCV; events from the chart-events endpoint
price-history.interpretation: Follower lanes sync one-way from the main chart, never two-way, because a sparse lane (IV, GEX) has fewer points than price and a two-way sync would drag the price axis to the sparse series range.
price-history.limits: Indicators are computed on the loaded window only, so an indicator with a long lookback is undefined at the left edge of a short window rather than borrowing prior history. Event markers depend on filing coverage and are sparse for non-US names.
price-history.name: Indicator and event overlays

price-history.formula: MACD = EMA(12) - EMA(26); signal = EMA(9) of MACD; histogram = MACD - signal
price-history.interpretation: The histogram is the useful part: it crosses zero before the lines do, which is the earliest mechanical read of a momentum turn.
price-history.limits: Lagging by construction. Whipsaws badly in a range, generating crossovers with no follow-through.
price-history.name: MACD

price-history.formula: each series fetched from its own source and resampled onto the chart timeline
price-history.interpretation: The reason this tool exists: it is the only place a single equity can be plotted against a macro series and a chokepoint transit count on one timeline.
price-history.limits: Monthly macro series step rather than move, so on an intraday chart they render as flat plateaus. Mixing frequencies on one axis is visually honest only because each lane is separate.
price-history.name: Macro overlay lanes

price-history.formula: SMA = mean(close, N); EMA = exponentially weighted mean with span N
price-history.interpretation: Both the type and period are user-set, so the overlay matches whatever convention the reader already uses rather than imposing one.
price-history.limits: Computed on the loaded window only, so an average with a long period is undefined at the left edge rather than borrowing prior history.
price-history.name: Moving averages

price-history.formula: 100 - 100/(1 + average gain / average loss) over the period, Wilder smoothing
price-history.interpretation: Above 70 and below 30 are the conventional extremes, drawn as reference lines. In a strong trend RSI stays extreme for a long time, which is why it is a lane and not a signal.
price-history.limits: Bounded, so it compresses information at the extremes. Divergence readings are subjective and not computed here.
price-history.name: RSI

price-history.formula: cumulative(price x volume) / cumulative(volume), reset per session
price-history.interpretation: The execution benchmark. Price above VWAP with rising volume is the classic intraday strength read.
price-history.limits: On the IEX feed the volume is a partial tape, so VWAP is computed off a subset of prints and will differ from a consolidated VWAP.
price-history.name: VWAP

rate-engine.interpretation: The Fed own projection against the market path is the interesting comparison; a wide gap usually resolves toward the market.
rate-engine.limits: Median, central tendency and range only. Individual participant dots are NOT plotted because they are not published as attributable data, and inventing them would be fabrication.
rate-engine.name: SEP dot plot

rate-engine.interpretation: The base rate structure everything else prices off. Shape matters more than level: an inverted curve has preceded every US recession since 1970.
rate-engine.limits: Constant-maturity par yields, not zero-coupon or forward rates, so they are not directly usable for discounting a cash flow at a specific date.
rate-engine.name: US Treasury yield curve

rate-engine.formula: yield(long) - yield(short) per pair, with a 6-month trend
rate-engine.interpretation: Negative is inversion. The 10y-2y is the headline; the 10y-3m is the one most cited in the academic recession literature. Both feed the cycle composite.
rate-engine.limits: Inversion leads recessions by 6 to 18 months, a lag long and variable enough that the signal is close to useless for timing.
rate-engine.name: Curve spreads

rate-engine.formula: CME Fed funds futures (ZQ), unblended for meeting-month timing; falls back to the FRED Treasury curve where a contract has no data
rate-engine.interpretation: What the market expects, not what the Fed has said. Meetings priced off the curve fallback are flagged in gold so the reader knows which are futures-implied and which are inferred.
rate-engine.limits: Futures imply a distribution of the average effective rate over the month, not a clean per-meeting probability; the unblending is an approximation. The curve fallback is materially weaker.
rate-engine.name: Implied FOMC path

regression.formula: cov/var beta; flagged when |CAPM - Scholes-Williams| exceeds 15% of the CAPM value
regression.interpretation: The divergence is the signal. A large gap means the naive beta is biased toward 1 by thin trading and should not be used for hedging.
regression.limits: The 15% threshold is a starting point for flagging, not a statistically derived cutoff, and the code says so explicitly.
regression.name: CAPM beta and the thin-trading flag

regression.formula: multivariate OLS of excess returns on the Ken French FF3 or FF4 factor set
regression.interpretation: Separates a return into style exposures. A "stock picker" whose returns are explained by a small-value tilt has a factor portfolio, not a skill.
regression.limits: Factors are US-centric and the library updates monthly with a lag. Loadings over a single year are noisy and rarely significant.
regression.name: Fama-French factor loadings

seasonality.formula: resample to month-end, pct_change, group by calendar month; mean, median, share positive, best, worst
seasonality.interpretation: Read the hit rate before the mean: a +2.8% average on a 55% hit rate is one enormous year, while the same average at 80% is a pattern. SPY comes out November best and September worst, which is the documented shape and a useful sanity check that the calculation is sound.
seasonality.limits: Ten to forty observations per bucket. No significance test is reported and none is implied. Month-end to month-end, so it captures the move you would have held rather than an average of daily returns, which would drop compounding.
seasonality.name: Average return by month

seasonality.formula: group daily pct_change by index.dayofweek; mean, median, share positive
seasonality.interpretation: Texture, not an edge. Effects are a few hundredths of a percent on samples of a few thousand days, and the page says so next to the table.
seasonality.limits: Differences are well inside the noise for any realistic sample. Ignores holidays and half-days, which cluster on particular weekdays.
seasonality.name: Day of week

seasonality.formula: flag last 1 and first 3 sessions of each month; compare mean daily return of the flagged set against the remainder
seasonality.interpretation: A long-documented pattern usually attributed to pension and payroll flows. The comparison figure matters more than the level: SPY prints 0.07% against 0.04% for the rest of the month.
seasonality.limits: Session-based, not calendar-based, so a month ending on a weekend shifts the window. No control for month-end index rebalancing, which overlaps the same days.
seasonality.name: Turn of month

seasonality.formula: monthly returns pivoted to year x month
seasonality.interpretation: The audit trail for the averages above it. Scan the column for a month before trusting its mean: one 2008 or one 2020 can carry an entire average on its own.
seasonality.limits: Partial first and last years appear as short rows, so the top and bottom of the grid are not comparable with the full years between them. Colour intensity is capped at a fixed scale, so two very different large moves shade identically.
seasonality.name: Year-by-year grid

sector-rotation.formula: quadrant from sign of (x-100, y-100); tail is the last N weekly coordinate pairs
sector-rotation.interpretation: Rotation runs clockwise, so the tail carries more information than the dot: a sector in Weakening arriving from Leading is a position unwinding, while the same dot arriving from Lagging is one being built. Zero sectors in Leading means no sector is out in front and the index is being carried by individual names.
sector-rotation.limits: This is the standard public construction of the graph, not a reproduction of the commercial product, whose exact smoothing is proprietary. Shape and readings are right; decimals will not match a paid terminal.
sector-rotation.name: Quadrant and tail

sector-rotation.formula: 100 + zscore(RS-Ratio.diff(4 weeks), 52w baseline), then a 3-week average
sector-rotation.interpretation: The y axis, and the derivative of the x axis: strength is position, momentum is velocity. Above 100 means strength is building faster than that sector typically manages. XLK reads 98.6 while still at 102 strength, which is a leader rolling over.
sector-rotation.limits: Also normalised against the sector own history, so a sector whose strength rose slightly can still print below 100 if it normally rises faster. Not a measure of volatility or jumpiness. Before 2026-08-08 this used a 12-week baseline and a one-week difference, which produced coordinates that swung 2-4 points a week and rendered as a mesh.
sector-rotation.name: RS-Momentum

sector-rotation.formula: 100 + zscore(EMA_10w(sector_close / SPY_close), 52w baseline), then a 3-week average
sector-rotation.interpretation: The x axis. 102 is roughly two standard deviations ahead of its own normal. Left of 100 is underperforming. XLK currently reads 102.0 on the back of +21% against SPY over six months.
sector-rotation.limits: Self-referential: both axes are z-scores against the sector own history, so two sectors at 101 are each two sigma strong relative to themselves, not equally strong in absolute terms. Cannot be read as "XLK beat XLV by this much".
sector-rotation.name: RS-Ratio (relative strength)

sector-rotation.interpretation: Positive means the last month outpaced the quarterly run rate, so the trend is accelerating. This is the simple sortable version; the RRG view is the same idea done properly with smoothing and a normalised baseline.
sector-rotation.limits: A crude approximation of acceleration that assumes a linear 3-month path. It will flag a sector that fell hard two months ago and merely stopped falling.
sector-rotation.name: Sector momentum score

sector-rotation.interpretation: The heatmap. Positive means the sector beat the index over that window. Reading several periods together separates a durable leader from a one-week bounce.
sector-rotation.limits: Sector ETFs are proxies for the GICS sectors, so they carry their own fees and tracking error. Eleven sectors only; no industry-level detail.
sector-rotation.name: Sector relative return

sector-rrg.formula: quadrant from sign of (x-100, y-100); tail is the last N weekly coordinate pairs
sector-rrg.interpretation: Rotation runs clockwise, so the tail carries more information than the dot: a sector in Weakening arriving from Leading is a position unwinding, while the same dot arriving from Lagging is one being built. Zero sectors in Leading means no sector is out in front and the index is being carried by individual names.
sector-rrg.limits: This is the standard public construction of the graph, not a reproduction of the commercial product, whose exact smoothing is proprietary. Shape and readings are right; decimals will not match a paid terminal.
sector-rrg.name: Quadrant and tail

sector-rrg.formula: 100 + zscore(RS-Ratio.diff(4 weeks), 52w baseline), then a 3-week average
sector-rrg.interpretation: The y axis, and the derivative of the x axis: strength is position, momentum is velocity. Above 100 means strength is building faster than that sector typically manages. XLK reads 98.6 while still at 102 strength, which is a leader rolling over.
sector-rrg.limits: Also normalised against the sector own history, so a sector whose strength rose slightly can still print below 100 if it normally rises faster. Not a measure of volatility or jumpiness. Before 2026-08-08 this used a 12-week baseline and a one-week difference, which produced coordinates that swung 2-4 points a week and rendered as a mesh.
sector-rrg.name: RS-Momentum

sector-rrg.formula: 100 + zscore(EMA_10w(sector_close / SPY_close), 52w baseline), then a 3-week average
sector-rrg.interpretation: The x axis. 102 is roughly two standard deviations ahead of its own normal. Left of 100 is underperforming. XLK currently reads 102.0 on the back of +21% against SPY over six months.
sector-rrg.limits: Self-referential: both axes are z-scores against the sector own history, so two sectors at 101 are each two sigma strong relative to themselves, not equally strong in absolute terms. Cannot be read as "XLK beat XLV by this much".
sector-rrg.name: RS-Ratio (relative strength)

sector-rrg.interpretation: Positive means the last month outpaced the quarterly run rate, so the trend is accelerating. This is the simple sortable version; the RRG view is the same idea done properly with smoothing and a normalised baseline.
sector-rrg.limits: A crude approximation of acceleration that assumes a linear 3-month path. It will flag a sector that fell hard two months ago and merely stopped falling.
sector-rrg.name: Sector momentum score

sector-rrg.interpretation: The heatmap. Positive means the sector beat the index over that window. Reading several periods together separates a durable leader from a one-week bounce.
sector-rrg.limits: Sector ETFs are proxies for the GICS sectors, so they carry their own fees and tracking error. Eleven sectors only; no industry-level detail.
sector-rrg.name: Sector relative return

sentiment.formula: shingle/Jaccard similarity over titles groups duplicates; the representative carries a seen_in_sources count
sentiment.interpretation: A story appearing across N feeds is weighted once, not N times, with an "N FEEDS" badge. Prevents a single syndicated wire story from moving the composite.
sentiment.limits: Similarity is lexical, so a genuinely independent story on the same event with different wording is not merged, and a rewritten headline can escape the grouping.
sentiment.name: Breaking headlines and cross-source dedup

sentiment.formula: a deterministic horizon classifier splits each headline, then forward and backward subscores are aggregated separately
sentiment.interpretation: "The news is bad" and "the news says things will be bad" are different claims, and only the forward series has any predictive pretension at all.
sentiment.limits: The classifier is rule-based, so a headline mixing a result and a guidance change is assigned one horizon. History is aggregate rather than per ticker.
sentiment.name: Forward and backward-looking sentiment

sentiment.formula: headline scores grouped by the asset class the lexicon assigns
sentiment.interpretation: A single market sentiment number hides that crypto and macro news frequently point in opposite directions. Four classes only, because FX and fixed income proved too ambiguous to score and were dropped rather than left noisy.
sentiment.limits: Assignment is lexical, so a story touching two classes lands in one. Commodities coverage is thin relative to Equities.
sentiment.name: Sentiment by asset class

sentiment.formula: lexicon scoring per headline, weighted by source reliability; low-confidence headlines (<=0.55) go to one batched temperature-0 LLM call that can override direction; aggregated to a composite
sentiment.interpretation: The lexicon stays primary and the LLM only corrects the uncertain tail, which keeps the score deterministic and cheap. Split into forward-looking and backward-looking subscores, and by asset class, because "the news is bad" and "the news says things will be bad" are different claims.
sentiment.limits: Reddit is configured with 8 subreddit sources but production returns one, sitting at the neutral default: Reddit blocks datacenter IPs, so any mention-velocity feature built on it would be measuring nothing. Asset-class breakdown covers Equities, Crypto, Macro and Commodities only; FX and fixed income were dropped as too ambiguous to score. History is aggregate, not per ticker.
sentiment.name: Composite sentiment score

volatility-skew.formula: ATM IV minus annualised 30-day realised volatility (the IV premium)
volatility-skew.interpretation: The variance risk premium in one number. Persistently positive is the structural norm; a negative reading means options are cheap relative to how the stock is actually moving.
volatility-skew.limits: Compares a forward-looking implied number against a backward-looking realised one over different windows, which is standard practice but not an apples-to-apples comparison.
volatility-skew.name: IV against realised volatility

volatility-skew.formula: iv_rank = (current - min) / (max - min) * 100; iv_percentile = share of days below current * 100
volatility-skew.interpretation: Rank answers "how expensive is vol against its own year" and is the standard trigger for premium selling above ~50 and buying below ~20. Percentile is the more robust of the two because a single spike sets the range that rank divides by. Also available as an alert condition.
volatility-skew.limits: Both need a year of accrued snapshots; a ticker only recently tracked has a short and therefore flattering range. There is no historical IV surface from any current vendor, so the series starts when this app started recording it, not when the option started trading.
volatility-skew.name: IV rank and IV percentile

volatility-skew.formula: ATM IV per expiry across up to 16 expiries, with the front-to-back slope
volatility-skew.interpretation: Backwardation, where the front is above the back, marks an event or a stress. Contango is the resting state. The slope figure is what the scanner sorts on.
volatility-skew.limits: Chain-derived and point-in-time. Expiries are unevenly spaced, so the slope between adjacent expiries is not a constant-maturity measure.
volatility-skew.name: Term structure

volatility-skew.formula: per-strike IV from the chain, normalised through one shared _normalize_iv rule; 25-delta risk reversal and butterfly reported alongside
volatility-skew.interpretation: A steep put skew means downside protection is bid, which is normal for an index and a signal in a single name. The 25-delta risk reversal is the compact numeric version of the same read.
volatility-skew.limits: IV is normalised by one shared rule because the two sources quote it differently; before that fix the same contract could read 25% in one pane and 0% in another. No historical surface, so today skew cannot be compared with its own history.
volatility-skew.name: Volatility skew
